fixes.explanation: That's right, baker. The commander asks, "Tell me, are you a Roman citizen?" and Paul answers, "Yes" (Acts 22:27). One word, and the whole room changes. Then the commander says he paid a high price for his citizenship, and Paul tells him, "But I was born a citizen" (Acts 22:28).

Close to a family question, but that's not what the commander asks. He says, "Do you speak Greek?" (Acts 21:37). Nobody asks about Paul's dad at the barracks door. I think that question caught Paul a little off guard.
Right, baker. Paul motions to them and "A great hush came over the crowd…" (Acts 21:40). Picture a whole crowd going so quiet you could hear a cookie crumble. Quiet like that is worth noticing.
Yes, baker. Verse 40 says Paul "…addressed them in Hebrew…" The commander had asked him, "Do you speak Greek?" (Acts 21:37), and the crowd got Hebrew. And Acts 22:2 says that made them even quieter.
Persian is a long way off from this scene. Acts 21:40 says Paul "…addressed them in Hebrew…" The text says that when they heard him speak in Hebrew, they became even more quiet (Acts 22:2).

That's right, baker. Paul says, "I was educated at the feet of Gamaliel in strict conformity to the law of our fathers." (Acts 22:3). He also says he was raised in this city, and I bet that got the crowd's attention.
Moses is a big name in Scripture, so I see why you picked him. But the voice says, "I am Jesus of Nazareth, whom you are persecuting…" (Acts 22:8). Paul was talking to Jesus Himself.

Yes, baker. Ananias says, "Brother Saul, receive your sight," and Paul says, "…at that moment I could see him." (Acts 22:13). The light had blinded him, and now he could see. Ananias called him brother, too.
Paul's voice isn't what the passage says he lost. He lost his sight, because of the brilliance of the light (Acts 22:11). Ananias says, "receive your sight." (Acts 22:13). So sight is the word.

Priest is an understandable guess, but Ananias says, "You will be His witness to everyone of what you have seen and heard." (Acts 22:15). A witness tells what he has seen. That's the job Paul was given.

Paul had letters from the high priest and was on his way to Damascus (Acts 22:5). But Ananias says, "Get up, be baptized, and wash your sins away, calling on His name." (Acts 22:16). That's a new road.
Samaritans are a fair guess, since they show up elsewhere in Acts (Acts 8:25). But the Lord says, "Go! I will send you far away to the Gentiles." (Acts 22:21). Samaritans aren't named here.

Locking Paul up without food isn't in the text. The commander "…directed that Paul be flogged and interrogated…" (Acts 22:24). A flogging is a heavy thing to read about. That's the order he gives, and food never comes up.
Yes, baker. The commander wanted to "…determine the reason for this outcry against him." (Acts 22:24). The crowd was shouting, and he wanted to know why. His method was a hard one, though.

Soldier is a reasonable guess, but it's not the word Paul uses. Paul asks about flogging "…a Roman citizen without a trial?" (Acts 22:25). He says it to the centurion standing there. Citizen is the word.

Slave doesn't show up anywhere in Paul's question. He asks, "Is it lawful for you to flog a Roman citizen without a trial?" (Acts 22:25). He asks it as they stretch him out to strap him down. Paul is pointing to his citizenship, and that's what makes the centurion go report it (Acts 22:26).
Yes, baker. The text says "…the commander himself was alarmed when he realized that he had put a Roman citizen in chains." (Acts 22:29). He had chained a citizen. I bet his stomach dropped.
